AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 6 1 Introduction Phobia and anxiety disorder have a strong impact on mental health and overall quality of life worldwide. While eective treatments exist a gap between the demand and

the availability of professional anxiety disorder treatments is prevalent Alonso et al. 2018. 9.8 of respondents from 21 countries were diagnosed to suer from anxiety disorders Alonso et al. 2018 within a 12months period. Although 41.3 of the diagnosed

perceived a need for professional treatment only 9.8 of all respondents actually received adequate treatment. Another study estimated the global prevalence of anxiety disorders with 4.05 and observed a sharp increase of 55 between 1990 and 2019 Javaid et al.

2023. With anxiety prevalence continuing to increase and a substantial gap between the perceived need for treatment and the actual receipt of treatment Alonso et al. 2018 negative consequences for aected individuals and society as a whole are expected.

The rst line eective treatment against anxiety disorders is exposure therapy ET Abramowitz et al. 2019 Telch et al. 2014. In ET a therapist helps patients confront their fears by repeatedly exposing them to stimuli or situations that trigger anxiety.

Throughout the process the therapist aims to change how patients respond to these triggers and to improve their ability to cope with anxiety. Typically ET is tailored to each patients individual needs and clinical history. ET is conducted over multiple sessions

depending on the treatment plan and the patients progress. In addition to anxiety disorders ET is widely used in the treatment of panic Meuret et al. 2012 stress Rothbaum Schwartz 2002 and obsessivecompulsive disorders Foa 2010.

Underlying ET are the paradigms of associative and extinction learning EL Craske et al. 2014. Associative learning is the process of acquiring an association between an unconditioned stimulus US which elicits a naturally occurring behavior or

unconditioned response UR and a neutral stimulus NS which would have not produced any response. After an association is formed the NS leads to a similar outcome as the US. Now the NS is called a conditioned stimulus CS which leads to a conditioned response
AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 7 CR. Extinction learning postulates that any learned association can be unlearned by repeatedly observing the CS in the absence of the US. Unlearning the association

extinguishes or lowers the probability of the CR occurrence. To study ET and its application in anxiety disorders it is common to use associative learning as a simplied laboratory lab model for fear acquisition and EL as a simplied lab model for ET Craske

et al. 2008 2014. The gap between the demand for anxiety disorder treatments and the availability of professional ET might be reduced by applying articial intelligence AI systems to automate or assist ET. One promising approach within this broader eort is reinforcement

learning RL a class of AI methods that model interactions over time between a rewardmaximizing agent and an environment Sutton Barto 2018. In RL the environment provides the agent with a reward signal at each time step encoding how

desirable the current outcome is with respect to the goal. The agents objective is to maximize its expected cumulative reward by selecting at each time step an action from a dened set that causes the environment to transition from the current state to another

subsequent state. Depending on the state transition dynamics and action the agent obtains rewards and adapts its policy to maximize its expected cumulative reward. A policy is a mapping from dierent states to actions . In other words RL seeks to nd for

each state an optimal action to maximize its expected cumulative reward over the course of interaction. Training an RL agent refers to its repeated interaction with the environment and the subsequent updates of its policy whereas testing refers to evaluating the learned

policy in terms of achieved rewards or the quality of the learned stateaction mappings. To date RL has been applied to improve medical diagnosis process control in surgical procedures drug discovery health management and the design of dynamic treatment

plans among other areas. In their survey Yu et al. 2021 oer a comprehensive overview of how RL has been used to facilitate or enhance various healthcare tasks. In an ET setting the RL agent could correspond to an RL therapist or a

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 8 decisionsupport system while the environment could comprise the patient suering from an anxiety disorder and all relevant clinical factors that evolve over the course of ET. In

this analogy states can correspond to the patients current condition approximated by selfreported anxiety levels psychophysiological indicators e.g. skin conductance heart rate or contextual features of the exposure situation. Actions can correspond to

therapeutic decisions such as which stimulus to present e.g. image of a spider or an instruction to think of a spider for how long and with what contingency relative to other events. With the overall goal of reducing or extinguishing the patients anxiety each

therapeutic action inuences the patients transition into subsequent anxiety states that are uncertain because they depend on both the chosen intervention and the patients individual learning dynamics. For each interaction the therapist needs to nd the optimal

therapeutic action to reduce the patients anxiety levels. Thus the reward could be any signal of therapeutic progress e.g. patient feedback measure of anxietylevel reduction and the policy could correspond to a treatment protocol and provide the therapists with a

mapping from the anxiety levels of the patient to therapeutic actions required. Conceptually RL is well suited for automating or assisting therapists conducting ET especially when using the simplied lab model of EL. EL reduces ET to a tractable

learning and unlearning task in which a CR that is anxiety is acquired and then reduced through repeated exposure to the CS. This simplication makes it possible to formalize ET as a sequential decisionproblem with dened states actions and rewards while still

capturing core mechanisms relevant to clinical ET. In this setting RL could help to nd the best actions for a given state to reduce the patients anxiety. Moreover through its policy RL could provide highly individual actions tailored to the needs of each patient and its

current anxiety state thus enabling sophisticated patienttailored therapeutic interventions. At the same time it acknowledges that EL does not account for all potentially complex cognitive emotional and social processes underlying mental disorders and thus using EL
performed by RL therapists serves as an initial exploration of developing and evaluating

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 9 RLbased therapeutic agents before extending them to more comprehensive models. In this setting the resulting system can be used in dierent ways. In a humanintheloop conguration the presentation of the stimulus is carried out by a

human therapist with the RL agent providing complementary decision support e.g. recommendations for the next exposure step. In a fully automated conguration stimulus presentation is delivered digitally on a screen or through virtual reality VR and the RL

agent directly controls the exposure treatment protocol. Previous research has already shown promising rst attempts to automate EL MahmoudiNejad et al. 2024 Tomasiak 2024. Tomasiak 2024 explored parameter congurations that allowed an RL agent to

perform EL on a simulated patient model that had previously learned associations in a twostimulus setting. A computational patient model was used instead of real patients and simulated their associative fear learning and extinction. Moreover MahmoudiNejad et al.

2024 used an RL agent to dynamically generate spider images that induced predened target levels of fear in human participants. Research Gap Nevertheless important research gaps remain on the path toward automated or

RLassisted ET. Firstly Tomasiak 2024 demonstrated that RL agents can learn to perform EL on synthetic patient models within an associativelearning and EL paradigm. Yet RL agents were trained to perform EL on simulated patient models without

incorporating established EL protocols or treatment strategies. For instance one standard EL protocol is immediate extinction in which the CS is repeatedly presented in the absence of the US. Incorporating established EL protocols might enable the RL agent to

learn more clinically meaningful policies. Data from past therapistpatient interaction might allow RL agents to learn from patient characteristics that have not been adequately represented in the current simulations like comorbidities extreme levels of anxiety
disorders or learning impairments. Moreover training on such past data could be particularly valuable in domains where data are scarce or costly to obtain such as in

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 10 personalized therapeutic interventions. Hence it remains unclear how RL agents perform when trained not merely on patient model simulations but also on data incorporating

established EL protocols or past therapistpatient interactions into training the RL agent and whether this would improve EL performance or generalization to previously unseen therapeutic contexts e.g. patient properties not reected in the simulation.

Secondly it remains unclear whether RL models can robustly learn to extinguish learned associations in contexts that dier from those used during training or the development of the RL therapist. To date no simulationtosimulation Sim2Sim or model

mismatch robustness research has examined whether an RL therapist trained on simulations derived from one patient model can reliably perform ET on other patient models simulations. In Tomasiak 2024 both training and evaluation of the RL agent

were conducted on the same patient models. In MahmoudiNejad et al. 2024 neither EL nor Sim2Sim was applied. However robust Sim2Sim performance is essential to determine whether reported EL outcomes are limited to specic models and settings or can be

generalized to patient models not used during training. Beyond simulations the present thesis hypothesizes that strong Sim2Sim performance may be a necessary precondition for reliable realworld application with patients who have diverse characteristics and across

varied contexts although this remains to be empirically validated. Given the potential risks that RL therapists might pose to human study participants and patients strong evidence of their generalizability across dierent contexts is required before RL therapists

can be tested or applied in studies involving real patients. Contribution to Research This thesis sets out to close these research gaps on the way to automated or RLassisted ET. It contributes to the literature in two ways. Firstly it examines whether

an RL therapist is capable of learning to perform EL tailored to the individual states of a patient model by using past patient model interaction data. Hence it explores the possibility of RL assisting or complementing human therapists and performs preliminary

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 11 simulation studies to evaluate its performance. Moreover it explores whether incorporating past data from established ET protocols into training can increase the rewards achieved by

RL agents indicating more eective EL performance. To allow learning from past data the opolicy RL algorithm can be used. Opolicy learning allows the RL agent to learn from policies that deviate from the one it is using itself. The past training data could stem from

previous EL protocols performed on simulated patients. In addition this thesis estimated the least required amount of patient data for the RL therapist to successfully learn performing ET. Hence this thesis constitutes a preliminary simulation study before

collecting real world patient data to optimize ET performance and is an important step to improve and apply RL enabled ET. Secondly this thesis conducts Sim2Sim experiments to evaluate the robustness of

the EL performance. Three dierent computational models of human associative learning were used to simulate patient behavior the RescorlaWagner RW Rescorla Wagner 1972 the KalmanlterRW KRW Gershman 2015 and the DirichletprocessKRW

DPKRW Gershman et al. 2017. In Sim2Sim the training is conducted on one patient model while its performance is tested on another. This approach allows for the assessment of the therapists adaptability across diverse patient parameters and models. A robust

performance might indicate low overtting to one particular patient model and demonstrate good performance on the other patient models investigated. Each model in use has its own advantages and limitations in simulating empirical human decisions and

behaviors. While the latter models KRW and DPKRW extend and generalize the RW model to resolve empirical inconsistencies all three are utilized in this thesis to enhance comparability with prior research. Moreover in this thesis a robust performance is

hypothesized to indicate a robust performance on other models not used in this thesis future model extensions and generalizations or real world patients with diering characteristics although this remains to be evaluated in future experiments.

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 13 2 Theoretical Background 2.1 Modeling Human Associative Learning and Behavior Understanding human learning and behavior is key in predicting explaining and

altering the behavior of patients. In the early 1900s Pavlov conducted his experimental research on animal learning Pavlov 1927 and introduced the framework of classical conditioning CC. Pavlov observed that dogs produced saliva as a biologically

predetermined response after seeing or anticipating food. Pavlov then repeatedly presented the food concurrently with a bell tone. Subsequently the dog started to produce saliva upon hearing the bell tone even in the absence of food thus learning the association

between the bell tone and the anticipation of receiving food. Quickly CC experiments became the standard procedure to study the formation of associations between stimuli or cues with their outcomes. In CC a stimulus that naturally elicits any behavioral response

is called an unconditioned stimulus US and its response unconditioned response UR. Learning is the acquisition of an association between a US with a neutral stimuli NS which previously did not lead to any UR. After the acquisition the NS becomes a
conditioned stimulus CS or cue and leads to a conditioned response CR which resembles the UR caused by the US. Additionally Pavlov observed that behaviors learned within an acquisition phase can

be unlearned in an extinction phase. After several trials of presenting the bell tone without food the dog produced progressively less saliva and eventually ceased its production entirely upon hearing a bell tone. Hence the dog unlearned the previously acquired

association. In CC an UR is elicited by a US naturally due to biological dispositions. In contrast a CR is a learned behavior occurring as a result of the repeated observation of an NS paired with a US and in turn it can be unlearned. Extinguishing a CR can be achieved

by the repeated observation of the CS when it is not paired with the US anymore. Each extinguishing trial tends to lead to a lower intensity of the CR until it eventually vanishes. Application of the CC framework in the eld of psychology proved to be a powerful

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 14 method to study human behavior. CC experiments with humans were widely replicated and resulted in similar learning patterns as observed in mammals e.g. Lipp et al. 2003

Mors et al. 2017 Nadler et al. 2011 Shiban et al. 2015 Talmi et al. 2008 van den Akker et al. 2015. The psychological paradigm of behaviorism aims to study and explain observable behavior without relying on the selfreporting of subjective inner

processes. Here the elegance of the CC framework became evident. It enabled researchers to study reproduce and variate human learning behaviors in a randomized and highly controlled experimental setting without relying on reported measures. Most importantly

for researchers CC posits clear predictable testable behaviors and association learning patterns. Expanding on the idea of predictability Rescorla and Wagner 1972 introduced a mathematical formalization of human learning the RW model.

RW Patient Model. RW quanties learning as the change of the associative strength between a stimulus and its outcome at a given time point or trial. In other words it estimates the learners expectation of a certain outcome given that a stimulus has been

shown. Each acquisition extinction trial tends to increase decrease the associative strength within the observer. The RW model approximates the change of the associative strength on a per trial level and can be viewed as a point estimator Gershman 2015 of

the learned association. Furthermore psychophysiological changes of the CR e.g. skin conductance pupil size heart period respiration and startle eyeblink are realworld indicators of the change in associative strength Bach Melinscak 2020. Hence the

learned association becomes testable after each trial. Moreover the RW model allows to reect dierences in learning across humans. Human traits which might aect learning or other dispositional factors could be reected in distinct model parameter values Pike

Dunsmoor et al. 2015 for review. The RW model and its proponents follow the idea that extinction is caused by weakening the learned associations until they are deleted or erased from memory Rescorla Wagner 1972. In contrast the PearceHall model Pearce

Hall 1980 conceptualizes extinction as the formation of a new inhibitory memory which competes with the previously acquired association determining whether to cause a CR. Although acknowledging the requirement of further integrative research Bouton et al.

2021 reviewed behavioral and neurobiological studies and concluded that there would be stronger support for the formation of a new inhibitory memory. While RW performed well in approximating learned associations and estimating their strength it came short in

explaining empirical ndings like the return of the CR and other empirically observable phenomena Miller et al. 1995. If an association between a cue and its US was truly unlearned a return of CR measured by a sudden recovery after days Quirk 2002 after a

short reinstatement presenting the US alone Haaker et al. 2014 or after renewal reintroducing the CSUS pairing in the original acquisition context or a novel one distinct from the extinction context Vervliet et al. 2013 would be inconsistent with the
predictions of RW Gershman et al. 2015. Reconciling the group of latent cause models LCM e.g. Courville et al. 2003 2006 Gershman et al. 2014 2015 2017 integrated both ideas with the observation that

processes the associative learning and structure learning Gershman et al. 2017. Structure learning postulates that learners attempt to minimize the uncertainty and complexity of their surroundings by inferring latent causes that are presumably causal for

the surroundings. In basic LCMs the learner observes sensory input such as a CS or a US and other contextual features. Each time step the learner infers a latent cause through a posterior distribution over potential latent causes using Bayes rule based on the sensory

input and prior learning. With each time point a new latent cause can be inferred and generated when the previous one seems unlikely to hold. Nevertheless a prior probability distribution favors few latent causes Gershman et al. 2015. The observed input is

evidence to the learners inference of the active latent cause. With two distinct latent causes the Bayesian learner can maintain two context dependent CRs for the same pair of CS and US Gershman et al. 2015. The CR occurs when the learner expects the

occurrence of the US under the inferred latent cause. A change in the context even when the CS remains present shifts the calculated posterior probability distributions over the latent causes and with it the US prediction.

with its predictions Gershman et al. 2015. If during the extinction phase the learner infers a new latent cause due to context shift e.g. sudden absence of the US the association remains in memory but is not exhibited anymore due to a change in the

inferred active latent cause. In this case the account of the new inhibitory memory holds true. However if the learner has no reason to infer a new latent cause the true unlearning of the CR remains feasible. The acquisition phase and the extinction phase need to be as

et al. 2015. Gradual extinction can be achieved by starting with trials where CS and US are shown concurrently and by gradually decreasing their frequency towards the end of extinction phase. On a computational level the RW model needs to be adapted to allow for

policy in the target environment. However it is often dicult to model the simulative environment representative of the target environment in healthcare. In particular it is challenging to accurately model POMDPs like ET where subsets of the target

environment are not observable and where research gaps remain to be studied. Zeroshot strategies are often accompanied by domain randomization the idea that randomly sampling all learning environment parameters might cover realistic parameter conguration

distributions that are present in the target environment Tobin et al. 2017 Zhao et al. 2020. In fact domain randomization was widely observed to lead to more robust RL policies in return for slower learning Tobin et al. 2017 Zhao et al. 2020. Another
method is the already above discussed and discrepancybased opolicy evaluation that

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 38 contrasts learned policys decisions with expert decisions from another behavior policy. In another approach for coordinated multiple RL agents the entire environments used for
learning in robotics settings were perpetuated to allow learning from deviating environments Tobin et al. 2017. Despite the grave need for safe and robust RL methods for clinical applications

healthcare specic RL robustness research is rare and most techniques are researched and sourced from unrelated elds e.g. robotics or computer vision. Nonetheless three notable exceptions were recently published. Firstly cross opolicy evaluation introduced

varying weights of single rewards during policy evaluation compared to the weights used during training Roggeveen et al. 2024. The rationale was that clinically benecial and robust policy would perform well independent of the used reward structure during training.

In addition the policy was restricted to not allow malicious actions during any state. Secondly with EpiCare a simulative environment benchmark was introduced to perform Sim2Sim and robustness evaluations of RL agents applied in dynamic treatment regimes

Hargrave et al. 2024. Dynamic treatment regime is an abstraction of ET and characterize any treatments where parameters like symptoms intensity or fear levels change and thus require patient specic treatment adaptation over time. Evaluation with

EpiCare revealed poor performance with high variability of RL agents in sparse data scenarios with limited observability despite a seemingly good performance with opolicy evaluation. DTRBench introduced an simulation platform to model realistic patient

responses and dynamic treatment regime dynamics to benchmark RL agents in Sim2Sim settings before evaluating potential performance transfer to real patients Luo et al. 2024. 3.3.3 Automating EL with RL

The most closely related works combined the abovementioned threads of literature to automate EL or ET e.g. MahmoudiNejad et al. 2021 2024 Rahman et al. 2022 Tomasiak 2024. A core challenge on the way to automated ET is to provide the RL
therapist with realtime biofeedback from patients or their observed CR. Rahman et al.

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 39 2022 proposed a framework to integrate realtime data into VRET interventions. Using electroencephalography they measured cortical activity and combined it with heart rate

variability to predict patients arousal or stress levels. They successfully demonstrated the feasibility of providing realtime feedback that an RL therapist can use to form treatment decisions in VRET. The next step toward automated ET would be to form automated

treatment decisions such as determining which stimuli should be presented based on patient feedback. To this end Tomasiak 2024 developed an RL therapist that interacted with an articial patient model. Based on the patients observed CR the RL therapist decided

which stimuli to present with the goal of reducing the CR. An important nding was that EL training worked best when delivered over episodes with EL 24 interactions yielding greater reductions in CR than longer treatment periods. Complementarily

MahmoudiNejad et al. 2021 introduced a framework in which an RL agent dynamically generated spider content for VRET sessions to elicit targeted levels of arousal or stress. By varying six stimulus dimensions locomotion movement proximity hairiness color and

size they were able to produce over 100 distinct spider stimuli and model patient arousal as a function of stimulus conguration. Together these studies seemed promising for applications in VRET. An RL

therapist could use realtime biofeedback from patients to estimate their CR levels and form treatment decisions accordingly. Subsequently it could generate stimuli designed to induce a CR of the desired intensity tailored to diering individuals and depending on the

chosen therapy strategy or the severity of the disorder. Importantly the last two studies relied on articial patient models. However in a followup study MahmoudiNejad et al. 2024 demonstrated that dynamically adapted spiders elicited higher anxiety levels in

human study participants compared to a calming condition. Moreover they showed that spider congurations could be tailored to elicit predetermined anxiety levels and that the spider stimulus to achieve the desired level varied across individuals thus supporting the

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 40 personalization of spiders to individuals. Notably their participants were not clinically arachnophobic and the study did not aim to assess therapeutic outcomes. Instead it

provided a proof of concept that RL based adaptation could generate stimuli capable of inducing specic anxiety responses. Thus fully automated ET has not been studied yet and its feasibility and therapeutic ecacy remain open questions.

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 79 6 Discussion The goal of the present thesis was to evaluate whether opolicy RL therapists could learn to perform automated and robust EL on simulated patient models. In

particular it was examined how the buer composition in opolicy RL impacted training EL performance and what policies were learned from past simulated data resembling dierent EL extinction strategies. Moreover it was assessed whether being trained to

perform EL on one patient model allows RL therapists to generalize their EL performance to other patient models and to diering patient parameter congurations during evaluation compared to training. For these purposes 4 experiments were conducted in

which the buer composition of RL therapists that were trained DQN models the buer size the patients simulative association model evaluation patient models and their parameter congurations were varied. 6.1

6.1 Q1 Training OPolicy RL Therapists on Past Simulated EL Data 6.1.1 Q1.1 The Eect of the RL Therapists Buer Composition on EL Across all experiments the RL therapists learned to successfully perform EL on

patient models. Using opolicy DQN models with prelled buers that contained simulated data from past EL interactions accelerated the RL training and lead to on average higher rewards than without past simulated data. While prelling the buer with

random lead to better performance this nding was confounded by the replacement of past simulated data by newer simulations along the training steps. Often the highest average rewards were achieved by the RL therapists as fast as after 10000 to 20000 training steps.

While 20000 steps would correspond to approximately 800 study participants when conducted live opolicy RL allows to reuse and learn from past patient data as demonstrated with the present simulations. The RL therapists achieved average rewards

were compared to the average rewards achieved by applying three predened baseline strategies. Across all experiments the RL therapists outperformed the baseline strategy of performing random actions which produced the lowest average rewards. Furthermore RL

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 80 therapists mostly tended to outperform the average rewards achieved by the strategy of gradual extinction. That strategy achieved the second highest average rewards and is

considered promising in preventing the relapse of CRs in the the aftermath of ET Gershman et al. 2013 Shiban et al. 2015. Lastly the RL therapists mostly reached a similar average level of rewards as reached by applying the strategy of immediate

extinction which achieved the highest average rewards. The two later of the three strategies are established procedures in EL experiments. Hence in terms of reward the RL therapists with prelled buers reached a comparable performance in the simulations to

the immediate extinction strategy that is frequently used in EL experiments. Importantly the RL therapists tended to learn meaningful policies that produced sensible actions during EL. Among RL therapists the best learned policies were mostly to

perform the strategy of immediate extinction. For a vast majority of observed CRs the RL therapists tended to perform the action 1 0 0 which when applied exclusively corresponds to immediate extinction. While immediate extinction is a widespread strategy in EL

experiments it recently came under suspicion of being involved in causing relapses of CRs Gershman et al. 2015 eectively counteracting the ET goal of long term unlearning of CRs. In contrast the strategy of gradually introducing extinction was found to better

prevent the relapse of CRs Gershman et al. 2013 Shiban et al. 2015 and is thus particularly promising for ET practitioners and RL therapists. Nevertheless in the present simulations the best known strategy when applied manually with a predened protocol

was indeed immediate extinction as seen by its consistently highest average rewards at the baseline comparison level across all three RW KRW and DPKRW patient models. Therefore the RL therapists learned to imitate the best available strategy to perform ET

in the environment and learning the strategy of gradual extinction instead would have been suboptimal. However since the strategy of gradual extinction is suspected to better prevent relapses of CRs in real patients future research could focus on how to train the RL
therapists to perform that particular strategy in order to achieve better automated ET

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 81 with real patients. In summary the RL therapists learned to successfully perform EL with sensible actions on simulated patients and the buer composition impacted the training

speed and EL performance thus demonstrating the benet of using opolicy algorithms. 6.1.2 Q1.2 Amount of Data Necessary for RL Therapists to Learn EL RL therapists using data from past simulated EL interactions during their training

improved their EL performance faster and achieved on average higher rewards than those that used initially empty buers. Moreover it became evident that the data of 32 patient models EL sessions each incorporating 24 patient therapist interactions was sucient to

reach a performance level similar to the default RL therapist versions having data of 4167 patient model EL sessions. Fewer data points were not explored as future realworld data collection would require a minimal level of diversity and sample size to ensure patient

representativeness. A potentially promising approach could involve rst training RL therapists with simulated patient models to enable full stateaction pair exploration then netuning and evaluating them by using real patient data in the buer. This would

produce RL therapists better adapted to real human behavior enhance safety and potentially increase patient trust. Despite relying solely on articial patient data RL therapists trained on a 32 patient dataset still achieved performance comparable to the

immediate extinction EL strategy and required only a modest amount of patient training data in the buer. 6.2 Q2 Robustness of EL Performance by RL Therapists 6.2.1 Q2.1 Robustness of EL Performance on Models Diering from the
One Used for Training Overall the RL therapists achieved a robust performance with consistently high average rewards. Moreover the performance remained robust when applying EL on the

other two patient models than being trained on. This was true across all the three patient models RW KRW and DPKRW. Although the patient models diered conceptually mathematically and in their complexity or number of parameters using them for the RL

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 82 therapist training produced remarkably similar actions for unlearning the CR. The nearly constant achieved average reward dierences across patient parameter congurations and

across the applied baseline comparison treatment protocols despite policies tending to produce similar actions suggest that dierences may be rather attributed to patient model artifacts than to a better EL performance learned by the RL therapists. Moreover if

performing 1 0 0 always was the best action a rule based approach might be more ecient than training an adaptive RL therapist. In contrast while immediate extinction is a well established EL strategy many ET manuals highlight the need of adaptiveness to

individual patients or contexts e.g. Abramowitz et al. 2019 Smits et al. 2019 Telch et al. 2014 and thus the RL therapists might have learned unrealistic therapist behavior that could be suboptimal or nonrobust in real world application. Therefore it remained

unclear whether the RL therapists would perform robustly on patient models that are more pronouncedly dierent or more empirically realistic and would require a higher degree of adapting the RL therapists actions. 6.2.2

6.2.2 Q2.2 Robustness of EL Performance on Dierent Parameter Congurations of Patient Models The RL therapists also performed robustly within a patient model. By randomly sampling the RW patient models learning rate and trying out dierent parameter

congurations for the other two patient models which can be seen as proxies for interpersonal dierences in learning behaviors a robust ET performance was demonstrated within a patient model in addition. Nevertheless the ndings on the eect of

shifting patient parameters are constrained by the missing domain randomization for the KRW and DPKRW patient models. On the path towards automated ET a robust performance within a patient model for dierent patient congurations is as important as a

robust performance across dierent patient models. Decisively for both within patient and between patient robustness the patient models must reect empirical behavior to enable the RL therapist to learn realistic patient behavior and the appropriate responses to it. It

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 83 will be essential to test the robustness of the RL therapists performance on additional models as well as on real patients before automated ET can be applied safely on a broad

scale in clinical settings. In sum in this thesis the RL therapists performed ET robustly within and between patient models. Nonetheless precaution must be exercised since the patient models used for evaluating the performance robustness might have not been
suciently distinct in particular regarding to the best found actions. 6.3 Limitations and Future Outlook Notably the ndings of this thesis are limited by its simulation approach that does

not consider real patient data the similarity and simplicity of the patient models in use the restricted observation and action space available to the RL therapists and an evaluative approach that may not have accurately captured longterm eects of unlearning

the CR. First the RL therapists in this thesis were trained on simulated data and performed ET on simulated patients. While the present simulations were inspired by real world EL experiments it is possible that crucial aspects of performing EL or unlearning

CRs were not comprehensively reected as no real EL no real therapist and patient interaction and no real patient unlearning CR data were used. Introducing real patient data in each of these components of future experiments might improve the simulation

increase the external validity of its ndings and increase condence in applying RL therapist in real world EL or clinical settings. Potentially RL therapist could be trained with patient models to perform ET well and then netuned with real patient data to

obtain an RL therapist that is more adaptive to realistic human behavior instead of articial patient model data. Such an approach would not only consider a more realistic data sample but could be considered more safe and increase the trust of potential patients

since human data was involved in training and evaluating the RL therapists. Second while the patient models diered conceptually and mathematically for instance by introducing a probabilistic learning assumption in KRW or by adding multiple
associations in parallel for the same stimuli combination in DPKRW it was demonstrated

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 84 that eectively they remained similar in regard to the best found action to unlearn a CR. The similarity of the patient models limited the generalizability of the RL therapists EL

performance and their EL robustness on other more distinguishable patient models might be impaired. Besides the similarity of the patients models due to simplicity the experimental design allowed only for learning CRs in a twostimulus setting. While such a

design with only few stimuli is common in CC experiments for EL it might have not captured the complexity of the mechanisms involved in clinical settings like panic phobias and anxiety stress or obsessivecompulsive disorders. Thus future experiments could

consider more distinguishable or more complex models to strengthen the applicability of their ndings to clinical settings. Third the ndings on the robustness of EL performance are partially limited by the

lack of withinmodel parameter shifts. In other words no domain randomization was applied in the KRW and DPKRW patient models neither during training nor during evaluation. A random parameter shift in the patient model could have better reected

interindividual dierences while still assuming the same underlying patient model. Nevertheless based on the domain randomization used during RW patient model evaluation and the strong similarity in the best policies found across all three patient

models it is expected that parameter shifts would not have substantially aected EL robustness. In addition the technique of weight variation between single rewards Roggeveen et al. 2024 was not applicable here since only the terminal reward was

nonzero. Evaluating RL therapist performance on the EpiCare simulation benchmark for longitudinal clinical treatment regimes Hargrave et al. 2024 could have provided further evidence for robust EL performance. However this was not investigated in the present

thesis. Thus the lack of domain randomization for KRW and DPKRW patients and the missing EpiCare benchmark evaluation constrain the present ndings on EL robustness. Fourth the observational and action space of the RL therapist may not have been
suciently comprehensive. In the present simulations the RL therapist relied on a

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 85 onedimensional observation space limited to patients CR. However in practice the data available to the RL therapist should be at least as comprehensive as the information used

by clinical practitioners when forming treatment decisions or selecting stimuli to present during ET Gottesman et al. 2018 2019. For instance clinical practitioners would consider the socioeconomic status comorbidities of the patient concurrently used coping

strategies or other health risks of the patient before forming their treatment decisions. Thus a multidimensional observation space should be preferred to allow the RL therapists to infer meaningful decisions considering all relevant data points. Likewise in the present

simulation the decision was limited to binary choices whether to select a stimulus or not. Yet in practice there is typically a broader range of actions available to induce an association. For example the association can be modulated by presenting only stimuli that

are similar to the original trigger of the CR altering the duration of exposure or by concurrently administering medications which is usually an option for treating patients that exhibit severe disorder. Similarly a CS used in VRET could be tailored to the

patients therapy needs MahmoudiNejad et al. 2024. Hence future experiments could consider a broader set of actions that more realistically correspond to the actions undertaken by clinical practitioners.

Fifth and last the evaluation whether the patient model exhibited a CR after EL did not accurately reect longterm eects. The goal of ET is to decrease the CR or clinical condition on a longterm or erase it entirely. Empirically the CR reappeared or

could be reinstated or renewed after a a seemingly successful ET Haaker et al. 2014 Quirk 2002 Vervliet et al. 2013. Thus it is essential that the success of automated ET reects longterm eects in the evaluation. However in the present simulation the passing

of time was modeled by a step or an action performed by the RL therapist. Longterm eects were measured as the subsequent ten steps after performing EL. Modeling time this way can hardly be compared to the human experience or to the CR evolution after months.
Furthermore next to other variables the longterm eect of ET should be accurately

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 86 reected in the reward function to allow the RL therapists to learn a meaningful actions Gottesman et al. 2019. However without a more complex modeling of time steps it is

not clear whether longterm eects were suciently reected in the used reward function. For instance the learned policy was to perform immediate extinction during EL a strategy which was suspected to be involved in the relapse of CRs Gershman et al. 2013 Shiban

et al. 2015. Thus the learned policy may have indicated that longterm eects might have been neglected by the RL therapists or were not properly modeled in the simulation. Future experiments may nd ways to better reect longterm eects in their simulations

AUTOMATING EXTINCTION LEARNING 87 7 Conclusion In this thesis the potential of automating ET through RL was demonstrated. More precisely it was shown that RL therapists feasibly benet from using past EL data that

stemmed from RL therapist interactions with simulated patient models during EL experiments that are lab models of ET. Moreover a robust EL performance was demonstrated within and between three patient models. Nevertheless the ndings were

limited by the thesiss simulative approach that lacked real patient data used three distinct but similar patient models considered for the RL therapists only a restricted observation and action space and was evaluated in a manner which does not compare to

human longterm therapy success after months. To advance the automation of ET future studies will need to incorporate real patient data use a broader set of patient models and train RL therapists that consider more clinically relevant variables in their treatment

decisions. To increase trust among potential patients and clinical practitioners and eventually pave the way for automated ET it will be essential to evaluate how the RL therapists perform ET on real patients in clinical settings.

ARTICLE IN PRESS Abstract Background The process of consolidating research through metaanalyses is time consuming and costly. Using textmining approaches to semiautomate the step of screening

and selecting articles eligible for inclusion might potentially save hours of workload and costs. A lack of evaluative research on the use of textmining for literature screening prevents the widespread adoption of textmining approaches among the psychology research communi

ty. This study explores the possibilities of applying textmining approaches to facilitate or semiautomate screening articles for inclusion in psychology metaanalyses. Methods The performances of two publicly accessible textmining approaches were evaluat

ed and compared against three recent metaanalyses from different subfields of psychology. Results Averaged over 10 textmining runs per metaanalysis across the three metaanalyses the approaches achieved recall performances between 62.5 and 99.3 specificities between

60.1 and 92.7 and saved between 54.0 and 92.0 of screening workload. Higher recall was observed when more articles were screened manually in the textmining process. Conclusions These findings suggest that textmining approaches can substantially reduce
screening workload while maintaining high recall. These efficiency gains come with a trade off the more workload is saved the lower the recall performance. Textmining can therefore

serve as a valuable tool for the initial identification of potentially eligible studies or as a sec ondary screening aid but the risk of missing relevant studies should be mitigated by retaining an appropriate amount of manual screening.

However conducting an MA is a timeconsuming and costly process 1. A big part of MAs is ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ARTICLE IN PRESS

pending on the numbers of articles that need to be screened 3. Therefore new approaches to manage this workload are needed. To accelerate this process and thereby reduce hours of workload and associated costs recent advances in automating literature screening have been

made using textmining TM algorithms. That is TM extracts information and patterns from huge amounts of texts and documents in a computerized process. Used for literature screen ing TM may reduce the amount of time required to create an MA decisively 45. However
TM approaches also tend to miss eligible studies 45 which makes their potential benefits doubtful. Also their relative novelty and the lack of technical skills and knowledge in the re

search community may hinder their application. Currently evaluations of the applicability and performance of TM approaches on literature screening are lacking in the social behavioral sciences and psychology. This may hinder the application of TM in the workflow of MAs in

these research fields. This study aims to evaluate if TM approaches can be beneficially used to automate literature screening for MAs in the field of psychology in order to minimize costs and the time spent on literature screening.

There are many promising TM approaches for literature screening e.g. 456789101112. The unifying feature of these approaches lies in the underlying task of text classification to assign articles to predefined classes 9 based on which articles will be
included in or excluded from an MA. A class could be any arbitrarily chosen category such as the use of the same medical intervention. Text classification could be based on titles ab
stracts full article texts and other information that is commonly reviewed during literature screening. Recently large language models LLMs have further advanced the capabilities of TM. LLMs
constitute a class of TM tools trained on vast amounts of data that can generate coherent texts ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ARTICLE IN PRESS
ARTICLE IN PRESS and dialogues and show strong potential for improving text classification performance. How ever LLMs are costly to develop and deploy require specialized hardware and their classifi
cation decisions are often difficult to interpret. Most importantly the use of LLMs may lack reproducibility as different runs can yield different results and access to models is often re

stricted 13. Reproducibility is a key requirement for transparent and reproducible research and the lack of reproducibility severely impacts the quality of research. In contrast conventional TM methods are computationally efficient can be run inexpensively
on standard hardware and typically offer greater transparency properties that are particularly important in resourceconstrained MA research where methodological transparency is valua

ble. Moreover traditional TM relies on explicit algorithmic and statistical procedures that allow direct inspection of features and decision criteria thereby facilitating reproducibility. Rather than being outperformed by LLMbased approaches traditional TM continues to pro
vide a robust and lightweight analytical framework that can function as a standalone screening aid or complement LLMs in hybrid analytical pipelines for literature screening in MAs.
Using TM for selecting eligible studies in standard literature screening processes has not be come common practice yet. Researchers first skim all titles and abstracts of articles retrieved
from a database search manually. If they suspect an article to meet the predefined inclusion criteria they note it down for later fulltext assessment to check whether it meets all criteria.
While it is often only possible during fulltext assessments to determine whether a study fully meets the inclusion criteria it requires substantially more time compared to assessing titles or
abstracts alone. The whole process is usually conducted with the help of digital tools or plat forms which sometimes even have integrated TM functionalities. TM approaches could ac
celerate the selection process. However their inability to detect all relevant studies and the lack of control by the researcher over the study selection are seen as key obstacles to broaden
acceptance among the research community 4. The completeness of the selected literature in ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ARTICLE IN PRESS

However as the completeness of selected literature is also subject to human error e.g. di verging interpretation of subject or inclusion criteria inattentive article screening too 14 TM approaches can contribute large value by preselecting relevant articles prior to manual
screening or by constituting as second screener. That is TM could be used to sort or prioritize articles that are more likely to be eligible for inclusion for manual screening 4 as is stand

a second screener it has the great advantage of one human researcher retaining control over the final study selection and process while substituting the second human screener 4. TM approaches could thus potentially cut the required screening time in half. While a computer

ized approach for screening does not guarantee the completeness of the selected studies it certainly reduces the likelihood of human errors through computerized counterchecking and could help save funding resources through increasing the human screeners efficiency.

ARTICLE IN PRESS Discussion The general aim of the present study was to examine whether TM approaches could facilitate literature screening in MAs in the field of psychology in reducing time and workload in se
lecting eligible studies. Further to contribute to identifying the best TM approaches two TM approaches were applied to three MAs from three different subfields of psychology. Perfor

mance was contrasted to the article selection of the original studies. The results showed that while the two TM approaches succeeded in saving time they also missed articles eligible for inclusion. For two of the replicated MAs the two best working approaches missed 1924

of all eligible articles while saving 8392 of manual screening time. For the third MA the two TM approaches missed only 14 of eligible articles but saved only 5459 of manual screening time. Contrary to our expectations TM recall performance was best for

Roberts et al. 18 MA and worst for Everaerts et al. 17 MA. However in terms of poten tial time saved TM application was more beneficial for literature screening of Everaerts et al. 17 than Roberts et al. 18 MA. Performance appeared to depend on the relative proportion
of all articles that were manually screened for the training dataset. Screening an absolute number of at least 600 articles resulted in a much higher proportion of initially screened arti
cles in the creation of the training dataset for Roberts et al. 18 than for the other two MAs. Overall while TM approaches substantially reduced the required workload they also missed
a considerable number of eligible articles. This suggests that TM should not be used as a standalone screening method but can either serve as valuable aid for human screeners for pre

selecting relevant articles prior to manual screening or serve as a second screener for MAs in psychology. Both TM approaches succeeded in selecting eligible articles for inclusion across different sub

fields of psychology reflected in an average recall of 80 reaching up to 99. Consistently both approaches achieved their highest average recall 97 for Roberts et al. 18 followed by Agostini and van Zomeren 16 75 and the lowest average recall 70 for Everaert et

call estimates are defined relative to the reconstructed datasets rather than the original MAs and highlight that the primary goal was to demonstrate the feasibility and potential of TM approaches for psychology MAs rather than to reproduce exact screening outcomes. Fully
